danish.title: Første bog (1805) — Kapitel 12
paragraphs: De eneste unge mennesker, der var tilbage i dagligstuen — bortset fra den unge gæstens datter og grevens ældste datter, der var fire år ældre end sin søster og allerede opførte sig som en voksen — var Nikolaj og Sonja, niecen. Sonja var en slank lille brunette med et blødt blik i øjnene, halvt tilsløret af lange øjenvipper, tykke sorte fletninger, der snoede sig to gange rundt om hovedet, og en gylden tone i sin hud, især på halsen og de slanke, men yndefulde og muskuløse arme. Ved sine bevægelsers ynde, sine små lemmers blødhed og smidighed og en vis koketteri og tilbageholdenhed i sin optræden mindede hun om en smuk, halvvoksen killing, der lovede at blive til en skøn lille kat. Hun syntes tydeligvis, det var passende at vise interesse for den almindelige samtale ved at smile, men trods sig selv fulgte hendes øjne under de tykke, lange vipper hendes fætter, der skulle i hæren, med en så lidenskabelig, pigeagtig forgudelse, at hendes smil ikke et eneste øjeblik kunne narre nogen, og det var klart, at killingen kun havde slået sig ned for at springe op med fornyet energi og igen lege med sin fætter, så snart de ligesom Natasja og Boris kunne undslippe dagligstuen.

»Ja, min kære,« sagde greven henvendt til gæsten og pegede på Nikolaj, »hans ven Boris er blevet officer, og så for venskabets skyld forlader han universitetet og sin gamle far og melder sig til militæret, min kære. Og der lå en plads og ventede på ham i Arkivafdelingen! Er det ikke venskab?« bemærkede greven i en spørgende tone.
»Men man siger, der er erklæret krig,« svarede gæsten.
»Det har de sagt længe,« sagde greven, »og de vil sige det igen og igen, og det bliver det hele. Min kære, sikke et venskab!« gentog han. »Han melder sig til husarerne.«
Gæsten, der ikke vidste, hvad hun skulle sige, rystede på hovedet.

»Det har overhovedet ikke noget med venskab at gøre,« erklærede Nikolaj, der brusede op og vendte sig bort, som om det var en skammelig beskyldning. »Det er slet ikke for venskabets skyld; jeg føler simpelthen, at hæren er mit kald.«
Han skævede til sin kusine og den unge gæst, og de betragtede ham begge med et anerkendende smil.

»Oberst Schubert fra Pavlograd Husarerne spiser med os i dag. Han har været på orlov her og tager Nikolaj med sig tilbage. Der er ikke noget at gøre ved det!« sagde greven, trak på skuldrene og talte spøgefuldt om en sag, der tydeligvis bekymrede ham.

»Jeg har allerede sagt dig det, Papa,« sagde sønnen, »at hvis du ikke vil lade mig rejse, bliver jeg. Men jeg ved, at jeg ikke duer til andet end hæren; jeg er hverken diplomat eller embedsmand — jeg kan ikke skjule, hvad jeg føler.« Mens han talte, kastede han med en flot ung mands koketteri blikke mod Sonja og den unge gæst.
Den lille killing, der slugte ham med øjnene, virkede hvert øjeblik klar til at begynde sine kåde spring igen og vise sin killingenatur.

»Javel, javel!« sagde den gamle greve. »Han blusser altid op! Denne Buonaparte har forvirret hovedet på dem allesammen; de tænker alle på, hvordan han steg fra fænrik til kejser. Nå, nå, Gud give det,« tilføjede han uden at bemærke sin gæsts sarkastiske smil.
De ældre begyndte at tale om Bonaparte. Julie Karagina (Julija) vendte sig mod den unge Rostov.
»Hvor ærgerligt, at De ikke var hos Arkharoverne i torsdags. Det var så kedeligt uden Dem,« sagde hun med et blødt smil.

Den unge mand, smigret, satte sig tættere på hende med et koket smil og indledte en fortrolig samtale med den smilende Julie, uden overhovedet at bemærke, at hans ubevidste smil havde stukket Sonja i hjertet — hun, der rødmede og smilede unaturligt. Midt i samtalen kiggede han rundt på hende. Hun sendte ham et lidenskabeligt, vredt blik, og næppe i stand til at holde tårerne tilbage og bevare det kunstige smil på læberne, rejste hun sig og forlod stuen. Al Nikolajs livlighed forsvandt. Han ventede på den første pause i samtalen og forlod så stuen med et plaget ansigt for at finde Sonja.
»Hvor tydeligt alle disse unge mennesker bærer hjertet på ærmet!« sagde Anna Mikhajlovna og pegede på Nikolaj, da han gik ud. »Cousinage — dangereux voisinage,« tilføjede hun.
Slægtskab er et farligt naboskab.

»Ja,« sagde grevinden, da den livlighed, de unge mennesker havde bragt ind i stuen, var forsvundet; og som svar på et spørgsmål, ingen havde stillet, men som altid var i hendes tanker: »Og hvor megen lidelse, hvor megen ængstelse man har måttet gennemgå for at glæde sig over dem nu! Og alligevel er ængstelsen nu faktisk større end glæden. Man er altid, altid urolig! Især netop i denne alder, der er så farlig for både piger og drenge.«
»Det afhænger helt af opdragelsen,« bemærkede gæsten.

»Ja, De har ganske ret,« fortsatte grevinden. »Indtil nu har jeg altid, Gud ske tak, været mine børns veninde og haft deres fulde fortrolighed,« sagde hun og gentog den fejl, så mange forældre begår, der bilder sig ind, at deres børn ikke har hemmeligheder for dem. »Jeg ved, jeg altid vil være mine døtres første fortrolige, og at Nikolaj med sit heftige temperament, selv om han kommer ud for ting — en dreng kan ikke lade være — alligevel aldrig vil blive som de unge Petersborg-mennesker.«

»Ja, de er pragtfulde, pragtfulde unger,« stemte greven i, han som altid løste spørgsmål, der syntes ham vanskelige, ved at erklære, at alt var pragtfuldt. »Tænk bare: han vil være husar. Hvad skal man gøre, min kære?«
»Sikke et yndigt væsen, Deres yngste pige er,« sagde gæsten; »en lille vulkan!«

»Ja, en regulær vulkan,« sagde greven. »Kommer efter mig! Og sikke en stemme hun har; selv om hun er min datter, siger jeg ærligt, at hun bliver en sangerinde, en ny Salomoni! Vi har ansat en italiener til at undervise hende.«
»Er hun ikke for ung? Jeg har hørt, at det skader stemmen at træne den i den alder.«
»Åh nej, aldeles ikke for ung!« svarede greven. »Vores mødre plejede at blive gift som tolv- eller trettenårige.«

»Og hun er allerede forelsket i Boris. Tænk engang!« sagde grevinden med et mildt smil og kiggede på Boris, hvorefter hun fortsatte, tydeligvis optaget af en tanke, der altid fyldte hende: »Nu ser De, hvis jeg var streng over for hende og forbød det ... Gud ved, hvad de kunne finde på i smug,« — hun mente, at de ville kysse hinanden — »men som det er nu, kender jeg hvert ord, hun siger. Hun kommer selv løbende til mig om aftenen og fortæller mig alt. Måske forkæler jeg hende, men i virkeligheden forekommer det mig at være den bedste fremgangsmåde. Med den ældste var jeg strengere.«
»Ja, jeg blev opdraget helt anderledes,« bemærkede den smukke ældste datter, grevinde Vera, med et smil.

Men smilet forskønnede ikke Vera, som smil ellers plejer; tværtimod gav det hende et unaturligt og derfor ubehageligt udtryk. Vera var køn, slet ikke dum, lærte hurtigt, var velopdragen og havde en behagelig stemme; det, hun sagde, var sandt og passende, og alligevel — mærkeligt nok — vendte alle sig, gæster og grevinde, for at se på hende, som undrede de sig over, hvorfor hun havde sagt det, og de følte sig alle utilpas.
»Med den ældste er man altid alt for klog og forsøger at gøre noget exceptionelt ud af dem,« sagde gæsten.
»Hvad nytter det at nægte det, min kære? Vores gode grevinde var alt for klog med Vera,« sagde greven. »Nå, hvad gør det? Hun er blevet pragtfuld alligevel,« tilføjede han og blinkede til Vera.
Gæsterne rejste sig og tog afsked med løfte om at komme igen til middagen.
»Sikke nogle manerer! Jeg troede, de aldrig ville gå,« sagde grevinden, da hun havde fulgt sine gæster ud.

english.title: Book One (1805) — Chapter 12
paragraphs: The only young people left in the drawing room — not counting the young lady visitor and the countess's eldest daughter, who was four years older than her sister and already behaved like an adult — were Nicholas and Sonya, the niece. Sonya was a slender little brunette with tender eyes veiled by long lashes, thick black braids coiled twice around her head, and a warm tint to her complexion, especially visible in the color of her slender but graceful and muscular arms and neck. In the gracefulness of her movements, the softness and flexibility of her small limbs, and a certain shyness and reserve in her manner, she was like a pretty half-grown kitten that promises to become a beautiful cat. She clearly felt it was proper to show interest in the general conversation by smiling, but despite herself, her eyes — from beneath those thick long lashes — followed her cousin who was about to join the army with such passionate, girlish adoration that her smile couldn't fool anyone for a moment. It was obvious the kitten had settled down only to spring up with renewed energy and play with her cousin again, as soon as they too could escape the drawing room, like Natasha and Boris before them.

"Ah yes, my dear," said the count, turning to the visitor and gesturing toward Nicholas. "His friend Boris has become an officer, and so out of friendship he's leaving the university — and me, his old father — to join the army, my dear. And he had a position all lined up for him in the Archives Department! Now that's friendship for you," the count remarked in a questioning tone.
"But they say war has been declared," replied the visitor.
"They've been saying that for ages," said the count, "and they'll say it again and again, and that'll be the end of it. My dear, that's friendship for you," he repeated. "He's joining the hussars."
The visitor, not knowing what to say, shook her head.

"It's got nothing to do with friendship," Nicholas burst out, flaring up and turning away as though from a shameful accusation. "It's not about friendship at all. I simply feel the army is my calling."
He glanced at his cousin and the young lady visitor; both were looking at him with approving smiles.

"Colonel Schubert of the Pavlograd Hussars is dining with us today. He's been here on leave and is taking Nicholas back with him. What can you do?" said the count, shrugging his shoulders and speaking lightly about a matter that clearly upset him.

"I've already told you, Papa," said his son, "that if you don't want to let me go, I'll stay. But I know I'm no good anywhere except in the army. I'm not a diplomat or a government clerk — I don't know how to hide what I feel." As he said this, he kept glancing with a young man's flirtatiousness at Sonya and the young lady visitor.
The little kitten, feasting her eyes on him, looked ready at any moment to spring into action and reveal her playful nature.

"All right, all right!" said the old count. "He always gets so heated! This Bonaparte has turned all their heads. They all dream of how he rose from a junior officer to become Emperor. Well, well — God willing," he added, not noticing his visitor's sarcastic smile.
The adults began talking about Bonaparte. Julie Karagina turned to young Rostov.
"What a shame you weren't at the Arkharovs' on Thursday. It was so dull without you," she said, giving him a tender smile.

The young man, flattered, moved closer to her with a flirtatious smile and drew the smiling Julie into a private conversation, completely unaware that his casual charm had stabbed Sonya's heart. She blushed and smiled unnaturally. In the middle of his talk, he glanced over at her. She shot him a look of passionate anger, and barely managing to hold back her tears while keeping up the forced smile on her lips, she stood and left the room. All of Nicholas's good spirits vanished. He waited for the first pause in conversation, then left the room with a troubled face to find Sonya.

"How plainly all these young people wear their hearts on their sleeves!" said Anna Mikhaylovna, gesturing toward Nicholas as he left. "[Speaking in French] Cousinhood is a dangerous neighborhood," she added.
The original French footnote: Cousinhood is a dangerous neighborhood.

"Yes," said the countess when the brightness the young people had brought to the room had faded, and as if answering a question no one had asked but which was always on her mind, "and how much suffering, how much worry one goes through so that we can take joy in them now! And yet the worry now is even greater than the joy. One is always, always anxious! Especially at this age — so perilous for both girls and boys."
"It all depends on the upbringing," the visitor remarked.

"Yes, quite right," the countess went on. "Until now I have always, thank God, been my children's friend and had their full confidence" — she said this repeating the mistake so many parents make who believe their children have no secrets from them. "I know I will always be my daughters' closest confidante, and that even if Nicholas, with his impulsive nature, does get into some trouble — boys can't help it — he'll never turn out like those Petersburg young men."

"Yes, they're wonderful, wonderful children," the count chimed in — he always resolved questions that seemed difficult by declaring everything to be wonderful. "Just imagine — wants to be a hussar! What's a father to do, my dear?"
"What a charming creature your younger daughter is," said the visitor. "A little volcano!"

"Yes, a real volcano," agreed the count. "Takes after me! And what a voice she has! Though she's my daughter, I'll say it honestly — she'll be a singer, a second Salomoni! We've hired an Italian to give her lessons."
"Isn't she too young? I've heard it can damage the voice to train it at that age."
"Oh, not at all too young!" replied the count. "Why, our mothers were getting married at twelve or thirteen."

"And she's already in love with Boris. Can you imagine!" said the countess with a gentle smile, looking at Boris. She continued, clearly preoccupied with a thought that always occupied her: "You see, if I were strict with her and forbade it... who knows what they might get up to behind my back" — she meant that they would be kissing — "but as things stand, I know every word she says. She comes running to me on her own every evening and tells me everything. Maybe I spoil her, but really it seems like the best approach. I was stricter with her older sister."
"Yes, I was brought up quite differently," remarked the good-looking eldest daughter, Countess Vera, with a smile.

But the smile did nothing to enhance Vera's beauty, as smiles usually do. On the contrary, it gave her an unnatural and therefore unpleasant expression. Vera was attractive, not at all stupid, quick at learning, well brought up, and had a pleasant voice. What she said was true and fitting. And yet, oddly enough, everyone — the visitors and the countess alike — looked at her as if wondering why she had said it, and they all felt uncomfortable.
"People always try too hard with their eldest children and attempt to make something exceptional of them," said the visitor.
"No use denying it, my dear — the countess was too ambitious with Vera," said the count. "Well, what of it? She's turned out wonderfully all the same," he added with a wink at Vera.
The guests rose and said their goodbyes, promising to return for dinner.
"What manners! I thought they'd never leave," said the countess after seeing her guests out.
